title: Magnetism
tagline: Moving charges, changing fields and light
summary: The magnetic force and field, Ampère’s law, Faraday’s law, inductance, alternating currents, Maxwell’s correction and electromagnetic waves.
overview: Magnetism is the force between moving charges. A steady current makes a magnetic field; a changing magnetic field makes an electric field; and once both effects are admitted, the fields can sustain each other and travel as a wave. That wave is light. This course is the experimental and conceptual path to that conclusion, at the level of the integral laws.

We start with the Lorentz force on a charge and on a current-carrying wire, then the Biot–Savart law and Ampère’s law as ways to find the field. Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law govern induction, inductance and magnetic energy. Alternating-current circuits are the oscillator of the previous courses, now made of L, C and R. Maxwell’s displacement current repairs Ampère’s law, and the last chapter derives the wave equation and the properties of a plane electromagnetic wave.

The right-hand rule is a convention tied to the cross product, not a law of nature, but you must use one convention consistently. Direction is where magnetic problems go wrong. Draw the field, the current and the force as three separate arrows before you compute a magnitude.
outcomes: Compute the magnetic force on a charge and on a straight wire, and describe cyclotron motion.
Use the Biot–Savart law and Ampère’s law for wires, loops and solenoids.
Apply Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law to moving conductors and to changing fields.
Find inductance and magnetic energy, and solve simple RL and LC circuits.
Analyse series RLC circuits in the steady state, including impedance and resonance.
State Maxwell’s equations in integral form and derive the speed and structure of a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum.

history.title: Oersted’s compass
history.detail: Hans Christian Ørsted observed that a current deflects a compass needle, the first experimental link between electricity and magnetism.

history.title: Ampère’s force law
history.detail: Within months of Ørsted’s result, Ampère measured the force between currents and began the theory that a magnet is a collection of currents.

history.title: Faraday’s induction
history.detail: On 29 August 1831 Faraday found that a changing current in one coil induces a current in another. The law of induction is the statement of that discovery.

history.title: A dynamical theory of the field
history.detail: Maxwell’s paper introduced the displacement current and concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave travelling at the speed 1/√(ε₀μ₀).

history.title: Hertz’s waves
history.detail: Heinrich Hertz produced and detected electromagnetic waves in the laboratory and showed that they reflect, refract and interfere as light does.

history.title: Magnets and conductors in motion
history.detail: Einstein’s first relativity paper opens with the asymmetry between a magnet moving past a conductor and a conductor moving past a magnet, which the Maxwell–Lorentz theory treats as different cases of one phenomenon.
